text.p: These are leading stories in this morning's Paris newspapers.

-- Eurotunnel channel tunnel operator reaches agreement with leading bank lenders on debt-for-equity swap at an estimated price of less than 22.50 francs a share. Banks may take over 49 percent of Eurotunnel capital, lower interest rates on pending debt reimbursements.
LES ECHOS
-- Financial markets registered record highs yesterday in Europe thanks to low rates and an increase in the credibility of European single currency.
LA TRIBUNE DESFOSSES
-- Prime Minister Alain Juppe wins parliamentary confidence vote, reaffirms vow to tackle unemployment, public spending.
-- Aluminium producers face plunge world in metal prices, Pechiney plans restructuring.
-- Government reconsiders high-speed TGV train building schedule, as Europe revises down infrastructure projects.
-- Auto parts makers expects flat demand in 1996.
L'AGEFI
-- Bank of France to restructure branch network, may cut number of branch offices.

-- Credit Lyonnais to report earnings today, after being granted a 3.6 billion franc state emergency package last week. State holding company overseeing the sale of Credit Lyonnais assets likely to ask for further state help.
LE FIGARO

-- Interview with Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi in which he says a Europe without Italy would be weakened and affirms commitment to Maastricht-treaty criteria. Says changing those criteria would be unrealistic.
LE FIGARO-ECONOMIE
-- Renault, Fiat and Ford carmakers chairmen at Paris Motor Show say automobile industry will cease to create jobs in the next ten years, but believe new industries will emerge.
-- Finance Minister Jean Arthuis says global economy is growing fast, and France's slow growth is partly due to sluggish investments and poor competitiveness from French companies.
-- Bollore Technologies and Belgian group CMB interested in taking over Saga transports group, may inject 125 million francs.
LIBERATION (Economic section)
-- TGV high-speed train program to be revised, government leans toward pendular technology trains which can travel at high speed on existing tracks, while TGV needs special tracks.
-- EU authorities look at French state help to textile sector that may create distortions to competitiveness.
THE INTERNATIONAL HERALD TRIBUNE
-- Credit Lyonnais's downfall from high-flying player to huge taxpayer liability has given it a reputation for being France's "worst financial scandal this century."
